lead: A blockchain network is a peer-to-peer overlay: nodes run the same protocol and connect directly to chosen peers, not through one central server. Each node stores and validates according to its role, and together they relay transactions and blocks. This design exists so no single owner can silently rewrite the ledger. You meet it in public chains such as Bitcoin, in consortium ledgers, and in test networks used before deployment. This chapter separates the roles—full, pruned, mining, light, wallet and seed—and shows how one transaction travels through a small network.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.6 on blocks and Chapter 1.2 on distributed systems.

sections.h3: The network as a peer-to-peer overlay

blocks.text: A blockchain network is not a new cable or router. It is an overlay: a logical graph of nodes that use the Internet to open direct connections to other nodes. Two nodes are peers when they speak the same protocol messages and can exchange transactions and blocks. The physical path may cross many Internet service providers; the overlay hides that path.

Each node keeps a list of peers. It may accept inbound connections, make outbound connections, or both. In a public chain, anyone with the software and enough disk and bandwidth can join. In a private or consortium chain, an administrator controls admission; the peer-to-peer links still move data, but membership is restricted (see Chapter 1.5).

The network is defined by shared rules: message formats, block validity, and the genesis block. A node that follows different rules is on a different network, even if it uses the same software; test networks therefore use a separate genesis block and chain identifier. A simple model is a graph. Vertices are nodes; edges are live peer connections. A node does not need a link to every other node. It needs enough links for messages to reach the rest of the graph by relaying.

A node is one running program with an identity (often a public key or network address) and a local copy of whatever data its role requires. The role decides three things: what it stores, what it checks, and what it serves to others.

head: Role
Stores
Validates
rows: Every transaction and block; relays to peers
Like a full node; answers old-state queries
Recent blocks plus current state or UTXO set (unspent coins)
New blocks; old block bodies may be dropped
Light or SPV node (Simplified Payment Verification)
Proof of work and Merkle proofs; asks full nodes for data
Keys and addresses, not the chain
Signatures it creates; may query a node
Nothing; it has no chain and only hands out addresses of other peers

blocks.text: Only full nodes enforce every rule without trusting another node. A light node trusts full nodes for data availability but checks that headers form the most-work chain and that a transaction is inside a block through a Merkle branch (see Unit 2). A wallet is not automatically a node; many phone wallets are light clients or use a remote full node.

Transaction propagation uses gossip. A wallet signs a transaction and sends it to one full node it trusts or operates. That node checks the signature, the format, and obvious double-spend rules against its current state. If the transaction is valid and pays enough fee, the node puts it in its mempool and sends it to its peers. Each peer repeats the check and the forward. Gossip is robust but not instant; duplicates are dropped by transaction ID.

A mempool is a local pool of unconfirmed transactions. There is no single global mempool. Two nodes may hold different sets because of timing, fee policy and connection patterns. Miners choose from their own mempool when building a candidate block. (The full transaction life cycle is in Unit 3.)

Block propagation follows the same shape. A miner sends a new block to its peers. Each full node validates the header, the proof of work or validator signature, and every transaction, then forwards the block. Light nodes receive headers and ask for proofs when needed. Propagation delay matters: a block that spreads slowly gives competing miners more time to find a rival block at the same height.

Network size and topology affect decentralization, but count alone is not enough. A thousand nodes run by one cloud account are not a thousand independent validators. Decentralization needs independent operators, diverse software and geography, and enough full nodes to serve data. More connections speed gossip but add bandwidth cost.

A test network is a separate blockchain with its own genesis block and worthless coins. Developers use it to test code and upgrades before mainnet. Testnet tokens have no money value; they exist to pay test fees.

spec.aria: A network: light wallet L1 linked to full node F1, F1 relaying to full nodes F2, F3 and F4, which are linked to each other, and light wallet L2 linked to F4. F1 to F3 are marked miner. A table below counts 4 full stores, 2 header-only wallets.

examples.question: A test network has 4 full nodes, F1 to F4. Three of them, F1 to F3, also mine. Two light wallets, L1 and L2, are attached to F1 and F4 respectively, as in the figure. L1 sends 1 transaction. (a) Which nodes relay it? (b) Which nodes validate it? (c) Which nodes store the full block? (d) Which store only headers? (e) If all 4 full nodes stop, can L1 and L2 confirm the transaction? Give counts.
steps: L1 signs 1 transaction and sends it to its attached full node F1.

F1 checks the signature and format and that the inputs are unspent (no obvious double spend) against its current state. If valid, F1 puts it in its mempool and gossips to F2, F3 and F4. All 4 full nodes may relay.
Miners F1, F2 and F3 may include it in a candidate block. One produces a valid block and gossips it.
All 4 full nodes validate the block and store the full block. Count = 4.
L1 and L2 store block headers only, not full blocks; a Merkle proof is fetched and checked per transaction and not kept. Count = 2.
If all 4 full nodes stop, no node serves headers or proofs. The 2 light wallets cannot confirm the transaction.
examples.answer: The network has 4 full nodes, 3 mining nodes, 2 light wallets and 1 transaction; all 4 full nodes validate and store the block, the 2 light wallets store only headers, and if all 4 full nodes stop the 2 light wallets cannot confirm the transaction.

traps: Assuming every node stores the whole chain and mines. Light nodes store headers; full nodes may prune; only mining or validator nodes produce blocks.
Calling a wallet a node. A wallet stores keys and signs; it may use a remote full node.
Saying a light node validates every transaction. It validates headers and Merkle proofs and trusts full nodes for data availability.
Treating node count as decentralization. Independent control, software and geography matter more than raw count.
Giving testnet coins money value. Testnet coins are worthless by design.

quiz.q: Define a full node and a light node in one sentence each.
quiz.a: A full node stores and validates blocks and transactions under the full rules. A light node stores headers and checks proofs, asking full nodes for data.

quiz.q: Why can a light node work without storing the full chain?
quiz.a: It stores block headers, checks the most-work chain, and uses Merkle proofs from full nodes to confirm that a transaction is in a block.

quiz.q: In the figure, L1 sends one transaction. Which full node receives it first, and which full nodes may relay it next?
quiz.a: F1 receives it first. F1 may relay to F2, F3 and F4; all 4 full nodes may relay after checks.

quiz.q: Why are 1000 nodes in one cloud account not equal to 1000 independent validators?
quiz.a: One account controls all 1000. They can be stopped or changed together, so they do not give independent validation or censorship resistance.
A mempool is a local pool of unconfirmed transactions held by a node before block inclusion. Each node has its own.

quiz.q: A test network has 5 full nodes, 2 of them mine, and 3 light wallets. How many nodes store the full block, and how many store only headers?
quiz.a: All 5 full nodes store the full block. The 3 light wallets store only headers.

quiz.q: If all full nodes stop, can light wallets confirm a new transaction? Explain.
quiz.a: No. Light wallets need full nodes to serve headers, Merkle proofs and block data. Headers alone do not prove transaction inclusion.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, node operation is a service: RPC providers, archive-node providers and indexers sell access to chains because running a full node costs disk, bandwidth and monitoring time. Research on light clients, stateless validation and data availability sampling tries to let small devices check a large chain without storing it. Search next for 'pruned node', 'archive node', 'SPV client', 'gossip protocol' and 'testnet faucet'.
